name: Photonic neural-network hardware and ML inverse design
summary: Any N×N unitary factorizes into a mesh of Mach–Zehnder interferometers (Reck and Clements decompositions). Programmable silicon-photonic meshes can therefore perform the matrix–vector products of neural-network inference optically. In the other direction, adjoint-gradient and neural-network inverse design produce non-intuitive waveguide, coupler and metasurface geometries.

name: Ewald summation: electrostatics on a periodic lattice
summary: Periodic simulations need the Coulomb energy of an infinite lattice of images, a conditionally convergent sum. Ewald splits 1/r into a short-range erfc part summed in real space and a smooth part summed in Fourier space. The leftover surface-dipole term depends on the dielectric condition at infinity; tin-foil boundaries (ε'=∞) are the usual choice.

name: Monte Carlo radiative transfer through turbid media
summary: Multiple scattering of light in clouds, tissue and dust is simulated as random walks of photon packets. Free paths are drawn from the extinction coefficient and scattering angles from a Mie or Henyey–Greenstein phase function. This solves the radiative transfer equation statistically where the diffusion approximation fails.
sources: Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)

name: Yee's FDTD scheme for Maxwell's curl equations
summary: The finite-difference time-domain method staggers E and H by half a cell in space and half a step in time (leapfrog). The discrete curls then conserve the discrete divergence of B exactly, and of D given charge conservation, a discrete-exterior-calculus structure. Stability obeys the CFL bound. FDTD and edge-element finite elements are the workhorses of photonics and antenna design.

name: Split-step Fourier solution of the fibre NLSE
summary: Pulse propagation in a Kerr fibre obeys the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, solved by operator splitting. Dispersion is applied exactly in the Fourier domain and self-phase modulation in the time domain; Strang splitting makes the scheme second order. This norm-preserving pseudospectral method also underlies Lugiato–Lefever simulations of Kerr combs and solitons.

name: Maxwell's unification and the speed of light
summary: With the displacement current, Maxwell (1865) derived transverse waves travelling at 1/√(ε₀μ₀). That speed matched both Weber and Kohlrausch's measured ratio of electromagnetic to electrostatic units and the speed of light, so light became an electromagnetic wave. Hertz's 1887–88 experiments confirmed it, making this the archetype of unification in physics.
sources: Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)

name: Electrodynamics of moving bodies gave special relativity
summary: Einstein's 1905 paper opens with the magnet–conductor asymmetry of Maxwell–Lorentz electrodynamics. He resolved it by making the Lorentz transformations, which already leave Maxwell's equations invariant, the kinematics of space and time. Minkowski's 1908 tensor form then made E and B frame-dependent parts of one object, so relativity grew out of electrodynamics rather than mechanics.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 891. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053221004](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053221004)

name: Are potentials real? Gauge and the Aharonov–Bohm effect
summary: The Aharonov–Bohm phase shows that charged quanta respond to A where B vanishes. This forces a choice: gauge-dependent potentials acting locally, gauge-invariant loop holonomies acting nonlocally, or nonlocal field interactions. It is the main test case for whether gauge symmetry is mere redundancy of description or physically significant.

name: Radiation reaction and consistency of classical ED
summary: The Abraham–Lorentz–Dirac equation for a radiating point charge is third order, with runaway solutions and pre-acceleration, and the point charge's self-energy diverges. Whether classical electrodynamics of point particles is even consistent, and how to read the reduced-order Landau–Lifshitz fix, is debated in philosophy of physics. Strong-field laser experiments now probe the same question.
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)

name: Rays as the stationary-phase limit; Airy caustics
summary: Geometric optics is the stationary-phase asymptotics of the diffraction integral as k→∞: rays are the stationary points of the optical path. Where two rays merge, the method fails at a caustic. The intensity there follows the Airy function, as in Airy's rainbow theory, which is where catastrophe optics begins.

name: Conformal mapping for 2D electrostatics
summary: In two dimensions the potential is the real part of an analytic complex potential w(z), whose level curves are equipotentials and field lines. Conformal maps, including Schwarz–Christoffel, carry a solved geometry into edges, slots and fringing-field capacitors. It is the same tool used for 2D potential flow.

name: Kramers–Kronig: causality makes ε(ω) analytic
summary: Polarization cannot come before the field that causes it, so the susceptibility is analytic in the upper half ω-plane. The dispersive and absorptive parts of ε(ω) are then Hilbert transforms of each other. Lorentz-oscillator models satisfy this; conductors need the DC-conductivity pole treated separately. Kronig (1926) and Kramers (1927) first derived the relations for the dispersion of light and X-rays.

name: Legendre generating function is the multipole expansion
summary: Expanding the Coulomb kernel 1/|r−r'| in powers of r_</r_> generates the Legendre polynomials, and the addition theorem turns them into spherical harmonics. Multipole moments are just the source's expansion coefficients in these eigenfunctions of the angular Laplacian.

name: Huygens–Fresnel principle as a Green's-function integral
summary: Kirchhoff diffraction comes from applying Green's theorem to the Helmholtz equation with the outgoing Green's function e^{ikr}/r. This turns Huygens' secondary wavelets into an exact representation. Kirchhoff's boundary conditions are inconsistent, which the Rayleigh–Sommerfeld Dirichlet Green's function repairs. Fresnel and Fraunhofer diffraction are its paraxial and far-field limits.

name: Waveguide and cavity modes as Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems
summary: In a hollow metal guide the longitudinal field obeys the transverse Helmholtz equation, with Dirichlet conditions for TM modes (E_z=0) and Neumann conditions for TE modes (∂_nH_z=0). The eigenvalues set the cutoff frequencies. The complete orthogonal eigenfunctions are the modes into which any guided field expands, like a drum head.

name: Retarded potentials from the wave-equation Green's function
summary: In Lorenz gauge each potential obeys a sourced wave equation, so V and A are ρ and J convolved with the retarded Green's function of the d'Alembertian. Causality selects G_ret over G_adv. Coulomb gauge trades this for an instantaneous Poisson Green's function for V.
map: \Box A^\mu=\mu_0J^\mu,\ G_{\rm ret}=\frac{\delta(t-t'-|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|/c)}{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

name: Statics as Poisson problems for V and A
summary: Electrostatics, and magnetostatics in Coulomb gauge, both reduce to Poisson equations: one for V and one for each Cartesian component of A. Coulomb's law and the Biot–Savart law are therefore both the sources convolved with the same Green's function 1/(4πr).
map: \nabla^2V=-\rho/\epsilon_0,\ \nabla^2\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J\Rightarrow\mathbf A=\mu_0\int G\,\mathbf J\,d^3r',\ G=\frac{1}{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

name: Coulomb potential as the Laplacian's Green's function
summary: The point-charge potential is the free-space Green's function of the Laplacian. Dirichlet and Neumann Green's functions, the method of images and separation of variables (via Sturm–Liouville completeness) are the general PDE tools applied to conductors. Uniqueness follows from the elliptic type of the problem.

name: Liénard–Wiechert fields and Dirac's radiation reaction
summary: Evaluating the retarded Green's function on a point charge's worldline gives the Liénard–Wiechert potentials; the 1−n̂·β factor is the Jacobian of the retarded-time delta function. Dirac took the radiation-reaction field to be half the retarded minus half the advanced field, a combination that is regular at the charge.
map: V=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{(1-\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\boldsymbol\beta)R}\right]_{\rm ret},\quad F_{\rm rad}=\tfrac12(F_{\rm ret}-F_{\rm adv})
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)

name: Jones calculus and the polarization coherency matrix
summary: Fully polarized light is a vector in C², and optical elements are 2×2 complex matrices that compose by multiplication. Partially polarized light is described by the Hermitian positive coherency matrix, which is mathematically a qubit density matrix, with the degree of polarization playing the role of purity. Birefringent principal axes are the eigenvectors of the symmetric dielectric tensor.
map: \mathbf E_{\rm out}=M_n\cdots M_1\mathbf E_{\rm in},\ J=\langle\mathbf E\mathbf E^\dagger\rangle,\ P=\sqrt{1-\frac{4\det J}{(\mathrm{tr}J)^2}}

name: Photonic bands as a Hermitian eigenvalue problem
summary: For lossless periodic dielectrics the master equation for H is a Hermitian eigenproblem, so frequencies are real, modes are orthogonal and a variational principle holds. Bloch's theorem then gives photonic bands and gaps, the same spectral theory as electrons in crystals. Unlike the electron case it acts on a transverse vector field with no intrinsic length scale, so scaling a crystal by s scales its frequencies by 1/s.
map: \nabla\times\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon(\mathbf r)}\nabla\times\mathbf H\right)=\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}\mathbf H,\quad \mathbf H_{\mathbf k}=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}\mathbf u_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)
sources: Yablonovitch (1987). "Inhibited Spontaneous Emission in Solid-State Physics and Electronics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 2059. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059)

name: The vector potential as a U(1) connection
summary: The gauge potential is a connection on a U(1) bundle and F is its curvature. Gauge transformations are changes of local section, and the Aharonov–Bohm phase is the connection's holonomy around a loop. A Dirac monopole is a topologically nontrivial bundle that needs two patches (Wu–Yang), and consistency between the patches quantizes charge.
map: A\to A+d\lambda,\ F=dA,\ e^{i(q/\hbar)\oint A}=e^{iq\Phi_B/\hbar},\ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{S^2}\frac{q}{\hbar}F\in\mathbb Z

name: Maxwell's equations as dF=0 and d⋆F=J
summary: In differential-form language the field strength is the exact 2-form F=dA. The homogeneous Maxwell equations are the Bianchi identity dF=0, and the sourced ones are d⋆F=⋆J. The integral laws are Stokes' theorem, the metric enters only through the Hodge star, and charge conservation follows from d²=0.

name: Transformation optics: geometry as an effective medium
summary: Maxwell's equations keep their form under any coordinate map if ε and μ are replaced by transformed tensors. A desired ray geometry, such as a cloak or a concentrator, is therefore designed as a coordinate transformation and built from anisotropic metamaterials. Equivalently, rays follow geodesics of an optical metric (Fermat's principle), the same mathematics that lets a medium mimic curved spacetime.
breaks: Ideal cloaks need singular, impedance-matched and strongly dispersive ε and μ, so causality and losses confine real devices to narrow bands or ray-only (carpet) versions.

name: Johnson–Nyquist noise and antenna temperature
summary: A matched single-mode antenna inside a blackbody enclosure delivers k_BTΔf to its load. That is exactly the available Johnson–Nyquist noise of a resistor at temperature T; Nyquist himself derived it from a transmission line in equilibrium. Radio astronomers therefore quote received power as an antenna or brightness temperature, with the radiation resistance acting as a resistor whose noise is the sky.
map: P=k_BT\,\Delta f,\ \langle V^2\rangle=4k_BTR\,\Delta f,\ T_A=\frac{1}{\Omega_A}\int T_B(\Omega)P_n(\Omega)\,d\Omega\ (h\nu\ll k_BT)

name: Super-resolution localization as parameter estimation
summary: PALM and STORM beat the diffraction limit through statistics rather than better optics. Isolated emitters are fitted by maximum likelihood, and the Cramér–Rao bound puts localization precision at about the PSF width divided by √N photons. Fisher-information analysis also shows that intensity imaging loses the ability to resolve two incoherent points as they merge ('Rayleigh's curse'), which mode-sorting measurements avoid.
sources: Betzig et al. (2006). "Imaging Intracellular Fluorescent Proteins at Nanometer Resolution". *Science* 313, 1642. [doi:10.1126/science.1127344](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1127344)

name: Faraday rotation (T-odd) vs optical activity (P-odd)
summary: Both effects rotate linear polarization. Natural optical activity comes from chirality (broken parity) and is reciprocal, so it undoes itself on retro-reflection. Faraday rotation is driven by the T-odd magnetic field and is nonreciprocal, so it doubles on the return pass. This symmetry difference is why optical isolators need magneto-optics.
map: \mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E+i\epsilon_0\mathbf G\times\mathbf E,\quad \mathbf G\propto\mathbf k\ (\text{activity, }\mathcal P\text{-odd})\ \text{or}\ \mathbf G\propto\mathbf B\ (\text{Faraday, }\mathcal T\text{-odd})

name: Inversion symmetry forbids second-order nonlinearity
summary: Under parity both P and E change sign, so every even-order susceptibility vanishes in a centrosymmetric medium. Second-harmonic generation therefore needs non-centrosymmetric crystals, such as the quartz in Franken's experiment or LiNbO₃. SHG is used as a probe of broken inversion at surfaces, at interfaces and in ferroelectric order.
map: P_i=\epsilon_0\chi^{(2)}_{ijk}E_jE_k;\ \mathcal P:\ \mathbf P\to-\mathbf P,\ \mathbf E\to-\mathbf E\Rightarrow\chi^{(2)}=-\chi^{(2)}=0
sources: Franken et al. (1961). "Generation of Optical Harmonics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 7, 118. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118)

name: T-breaking and absent Kramers protection for photons
summary: Photonic Chern insulators with one-way edge modes need broken time reversal, from gyromagnetic or time-modulated media. Photons are bosons with Θ²=+1, so they lack the Kramers degeneracy that protects electronic Z₂ topological insulators. Photonic 'quantum spin Hall' analogues instead use engineered pseudo-spins, which symmetry-breaking defects can couple.
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Poincaré sphere: SU(2) on Jones vectors, SO(3) on Stokes
summary: Lossless polarization optics act on Jones vectors as SU(2), up to a global phase. The 2-to-1 homomorphism maps this to SO(3) rotations of the Stokes vector on the Poincaré sphere, the same structure as spin-½ on the Bloch sphere. A closed loop on the sphere gives the Pancharatnam geometric phase, equal to half the enclosed solid angle.
map: U=e^{-i\theta\,\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma/2}\mapsto R_{\hat{\mathbf n}}(\theta)\in SO(3),\ \mathbf S\propto\mathbf E^\dagger\boldsymbol\sigma\mathbf E,\ |\gamma_P|=\Omega/2

name: The field tensor as the (1,0)⊕(0,1) Lorentz representation
summary: Under the Lorentz group, F_{μν} splits into self-dual and anti-self-dual parts, the Riemann–Silberstein vectors E±icB, which transform as (1,0) and (0,1). Its two invariants are E²−c²B² and E·B. In Wigner's classification the photon is the massless helicity ±1 representation of the Poincaré group.
map:
\mathbf F_\pm=\mathbf E\pm ic\mathbf B\in(1,0),(0,1);\ F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}=2(B^2-E^2/c^2),\ F_{\mu
u}	ilde F^{\mu
u}\propto\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B
sources: Wigner (1939). "On Unitary Representations of the Inhomogeneous Lorentz Group". *Ann. Math.* 40, 149. [doi:10.2307/1968551](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968551)

name: Multipole moments as irreducible SO(3) tensors
summary: The 2l+1 spherical moments of order l form an irreducible representation of the rotation group, so a rank-l Cartesian moment reduces to its symmetric traceless part. The Wigner–Eckart theorem then gives the selection rules for multipole radiation. It also forbids moments of order l>2j in a state of angular momentum j, so a spin-½ particle has no quadrupole moment.

name: Spin and orbital angular momentum of light
summary: Rotational invariance gives the electromagnetic field a conserved angular momentum. For paraxial beams it splits into a spin part fixed by circular polarization (±ħ per photon, seen as torque on a wave plate by Beth in 1936) and an orbital part from helical phase fronts (ℓħ in Laguerre–Gauss beams). For general fields the split is gauge-sensitive and still debated.
map: \mathbf J=\epsilon_0\!\int\mathbf r\times(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)\,d^3r=\epsilon_0\!\int\big[E_i(\mathbf r\times\nabla)A_i+\mathbf E\times\mathbf A\big]d^3r\ (\text{Coulomb gauge})
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Conservation laws of electrodynamics as Noether currents
summary: The continuity equation is the Noether current of the U(1) phase symmetry of charged matter. Poynting's theorem and the Maxwell stress tensor are components of the field's (Belinfante-symmetrized) energy–momentum tensor, which comes from spacetime translations. By Noether's second theorem, local gauge invariance makes charge conservation an identity that Maxwell's equations themselves require.
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)
Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)

name: Phase matching as momentum conservation
summary: Translation invariance of a homogeneous crystal conserves photon momentum in wave mixing, so efficient conversion needs Δk=0, usually reached through birefringence. Quasi-phase-matching deliberately reduces continuous to discrete translation symmetry with periodic poling. Momentum is then conserved only up to the grating's reciprocal vector.

name: Plasma frequency as photon mass: Anderson's Higgs route
summary: In a collisionless Drude medium, transverse light obeys ω²=ω_p²+c²k², a massive Klein–Gordon dispersion. The long-range Coulomb force lifts the would-be acoustic density mode to the plasmon at ω_p. Anderson used this plasma picture to argue that a gauge field can gain mass by absorbing a would-be Goldstone mode, the core of the Higgs–Anderson mechanism.
breaks: A normal plasma has no condensate and no broken symmetry. A collisionless plasma only freezes in static magnetic flux, like a perfect conductor, while a superconductor expels it (Meissner effect) because its photon mass comes from a phase-coherent condensate. With collisions, static fields penetrate fully.

name: Laser threshold as spontaneous U(1) phase breaking
summary: Near threshold the single-mode field amplitude obeys a Landau-like equation. Below threshold only zero field is stable; above it there is a ring of states with fixed amplitude and arbitrary phase. The phase is then a Goldstone-like soft mode, and its diffusion under spontaneous-emission noise sets the Schawlow–Townes linewidth.
breaks: A laser is an open, driven-dissipative system rather than an equilibrium ground state. A single mode is effectively zero-dimensional, so the phase diffuses freely (finite linewidth). There is no true long-range order or thermodynamic singularity, only a crossover that sharpens with photon number.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Rayleigh's λ⁻⁴ law from dimensional analysis
summary: Rayleigh (1871) argued that for a particle much smaller than the wavelength, the scattered amplitude is proportional to its volume and falls off as 1/r. Dimensional consistency then forces a 1/λ² factor in amplitude, hence λ⁻⁴ in intensity, which is why the sky is blue. It is the textbook example of a scaling argument.
breaks: It holds only for size parameter 2πa/λ≪1 and away from resonances. For a≳λ the full Mie solution, with its resonances and nearly wavelength-independent scattering, takes over (white clouds).
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)
Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)

name: Mode-locked frequency combs as rulers for constants
summary: A mode-locked laser emits a comb of evenly spaced frequencies, and f–2f self-referencing fixes its offset. This links optical frequencies to the caesium microwave standard, enabling hydrogen spectroscopy for the Rydberg constant and optical-clock limits on drifts of α. Earlier laser frequency and wavelength measurements had already led to fixing c exactly in 1983.
sources: Tiesinga et al. (2021). "CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants: 2018". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 93, 025010. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010)

name: Ampere redefinition: μ0 became a measured constant
summary: Until 2019 the ampere was defined by the magnetostatic force between parallel wires, which fixed μ0=4π×10⁻⁷ N A⁻² exactly. Fixing e and h instead makes μ0 a measured quantity tied to the fine-structure constant. CODATA 2022 gives μ0=1.256 637 061 27(20)×10⁻⁶ N A⁻², within 1σ of the old exact value.
sources: Stock et al. (2019). "The revision of the SI—the result of three decades of progress in metrology". *Metrologia* 56, 022001. [doi:10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013](https://doi.org/10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013)

name: Linear canonical transforms in Fresnel optics
summary: Paraxial propagation through any ABCD system is the Collins integral, which is the wave (metaplectic) representation of the linear canonical transformation given by the symplectic ray matrix. Free space acts as a Fresnel transform and a thin lens as a quadratic phase. A graded-index medium, whose ray Hamiltonian is a harmonic oscillator, performs a fractional Fourier transform that becomes the full Fourier transform after a quarter period.
breaks: The correspondence is exact only in the paraxial limit. Aberrations make the ray map nonlinear, and the wave propagator then stops being a simple metaplectic integral.

name: Eikonal equation is the Hamilton–Jacobi equation
summary: The wavefronts S=const of the eikonal equation |∇S|²=n² are level sets of Hamilton's characteristic function, and rays are its characteristics. Hamilton built this characteristic-function method for optics and carried it over to dynamics in 1834–35. Schrödinger later completed this optico-mechanical analogy into wave mechanics.
map:
|
abla S|^2=n^2(\mathbf r)\ \leftrightarrow\ |
abla W|^2=2m(E-V);\quad 	ext{rays}\parallel
abla S\ \leftrightarrow\ \mathbf p=
abla W
breaks: Both solutions become multivalued at caustics and focal points. There geometric optics fails, and diffraction (or Maslov phases, in semiclassics) must be added.
sources: Hamilton (1834). "On a General Method in Dynamics". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 124, 247. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1834.0017](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1834.0017)
Hamilton (1835). "Second Essay on a General Method in Dynamics". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 125, 95. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1835.0009](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1835.0009)

name: Ray optics as Hamiltonian flow; étendue as Liouville
summary: If the optical axis z is taken as time, rays obey Hamilton's equations with H=−√(n²−p²) and transverse momentum p=n sinθ. Paraxial ABCD matrices are symplectic in the reduced variables (y, nθ). Conservation of étendue and radiance is Liouville's theorem, and it caps solar concentration at n²/sin²θ_sun.
map: H=-\sqrt{n^2(\mathbf q,z)-\mathbf p^2};\ M^TJM=J\ (\det M=1\text{ in }(y,n\theta));\ n^2\,dA\,d\Omega=\text{const}
breaks: Liouville's theorem holds only for lossless systems without scattering. Diffraction blurs the phase-space picture at the scale of λ, where the Wigner function replaces the ray density.

name: Charged-particle Lagrangian and minimal coupling
summary: The Lorentz force follows from Lagrange's equations with the velocity-dependent potential U=q(φ−v·A), and the canonical momentum p=mv+qA differs from the kinetic momentum. A gauge transformation adds the total derivative q dχ/dt to L and leaves the motion unchanged. This is the classical root of gauge invariance and of the Aharonov–Bohm phase q∮A·dl/ħ.
map: L=\tfrac12mv^2-q\phi+q\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf A;\ \mathbf p=m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A;\ H=\frac{(\mathbf p-q\mathbf A)^2}{2m}+q\phi;\ L\to L+q\frac{d\chi}{dt}
breaks: Classically only the fields matter. That the potentials themselves have physical effects (the Aharonov–Bohm effect) appears only in quantum mechanics.

name: Fermat's principle and the principle of least action
summary: Light rays make the optical path stationary in the same way that mechanical trajectories make the action stationary. In Maupertuis' form δ∫p ds=0, ray optics maps onto mechanics with the refractive index in the role of momentum, so Snell's law becomes conservation of momentum parallel to the interface.
breaks: The map holds at fixed energy, which means a single frequency. The particle's speed is proportional to n, while light's phase velocity is c/n. Hamilton and de Broglie resolved this mismatch by distinguishing phase velocity from group velocity.
sources: Hamilton (1834). "On a General Method in Dynamics". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 124, 247. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1834.0017](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1834.0017)

name: Maxwell's equations from a field action
summary: Extending Hamilton's principle to fields, the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations come out as the Euler–Lagrange equations of the covariant action, and the homogeneous pair is the Bianchi identity of F=dA. Noether's theorem applied to this action gives the energy–momentum tensor. Gauge invariance of the coupling forces charge conservation.
breaks: The canonical Noether tensor is neither symmetric nor gauge invariant and needs the Belinfante improvement. The action also does not settle radiation reaction for point charges.

name: Photoelasticity: stress made visible by birefringence
summary: Stress makes a transparent solid birefringent in proportion to the difference of principal stresses (the stress-optic law, Brewster 1816). Viewed between crossed polarizers, a loaded model shows isochromatic fringes of σ1−σ2 and isoclinics along the principal directions, the classic tool of experimental stress analysis. The same photoelastic tensor drives acousto-optic modulators.
breaks: The method gives only stress differences and directions integrated through the thickness. Separating the individual principal stresses, or handling 3D bodies, needs extra methods such as stress freezing or scattered-light photoelasticity.

name: Elastic-solid aether and the Maxwell stress tensor
summary: Fresnel's transverse light waves led Cauchy, Green and MacCullagh to model light as waves in an elastic solid, and MacCullagh's rotationally elastic aether gave equations equivalent to Maxwell's in vacuum. Maxwell expressed electromagnetic forces as stresses in a medium. That is the origin of the stress tensor whose divergence gives the force density.
breaks: An ordinary elastic solid also carries longitudinal waves, which light lacks; this problem sank most elastic-aether theories. Relativity later removed the medium altogether.
sources: Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)

name: Vortex Biot–Savart law: vorticity as current
summary: An incompressible velocity field obeys ∇·u=0 and ∇×u=ω, the same equations as B with source μ0J. Vortex lines therefore induce velocity by the Biot–Savart law: a line vortex acts like a straight wire and a vortex ring like a current loop. Maxwell's 1861 molecular-vortex model ran the analogy the other way, to picture magnetic fields.
map: \mathbf u=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\boldsymbol\omega'\times\mathbf R}{R^3}dV'\ \leftrightarrow\ \mathbf B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{\mathbf J'\times\mathbf R}{R^3}dV',\ \mathbf R=\mathbf r-\mathbf r'
breaks: Vorticity is carried along and stretched by the velocity it induces (Helmholtz's laws), so vortex dynamics is nonlinear, whereas currents are prescribed. Parallel vortices of the same sign orbit each other instead of attracting the way parallel currents do.

name: Analogue event horizons in flows and optical fibres
summary: Sound in an irrotational flow travels on an effective acoustic metric, with a horizon where the flow outruns sound. In a fibre, the Kerr index front of a soliton moving at the group velocity acts as a horizon for probe light. Both therefore serve as analogue-gravity platforms for Hawking-type mode conversion.
map: ds^2\propto-(c_s^2-v^2)dt^2-2\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf x\,dt+d\mathbf x^2;\quad \text{horizon at }|v|=c_s
breaks: Both rely on dispersion near the horizon. The fibre horizon is a moving index perturbation in a dispersive medium, not a flow, and claims of spontaneous Hawking-like emission in optics remain debated.

name: Hydrodynamics of light via the Madelung transform
summary: Writing the paraxial Kerr field as √ρ e^{iφ} turns the NLS into continuity and Euler equations for a compressible fluid. The nonlinearity supplies a pressure, and diffraction supplies a dispersive 'quantum pressure'. Defocusing media then show superfluid-like flow of light, optical vortices, and dispersive shock waves similar to undular bores.
map:

breaks: Propagation distance plays the role of time, and the fluid is inviscid with dispersion as its only regularization, so its shocks are oscillatory rather than viscous. Absorption and nonlocal nonlinearity break the analogy.

name: Optical tweezers: Rayleigh-dipole force in a Stokes fluid
summary: A small dielectric bead is a Rayleigh scatterer. Its induced dipole is pulled up the intensity gradient while radiation pressure pushes it along the beam. In water it moves as an overdamped Brownian particle with Stokes drag, so the trap stiffness can be calibrated from the Lorentzian corner frequency. This makes tweezers a force probe for microfluidics and biophysics.
breaks: Beads comparable to λ need Mie or ray-optics force calculations. Near walls the Stokes drag increases (Faxén corrections).
sources: Ashkin (1970). "Acceleration and Trapping of Particles by Radiation Pressure". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 24, 156. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156)

name: Atmospheric seeing: Kolmogorov turbulence limits coherence
summary: Kolmogorov scaling of temperature fluctuations makes the refractive-index structure function grow as r^(2/3), so starlight picks up a phase structure function proportional to (r/r0)^(5/3). The Fried parameter r0 sets the spatial coherence length and limits telescope resolution to about λ/r0. The result is speckle, which motivated speckle interferometry and adaptive optics.
breaks: Real atmospheric turbulence has finite outer and inner scales and is intermittent, so the 5/3 law fails at the largest and smallest separations.
sources: Kolmogorov (1941; English translation 1991). "The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 434, 9. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1991.0075](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1991.0075)

name: Inverse-square law: Kepler orbits and Coulomb fields
summary: Newtonian gravity and electrostatics share Poisson's equation and the 1/r Green's function. Gauss's law, the shell theorem and the conserved Runge–Lenz vector therefore carry over between them. Rutherford scattering is the hyperbolic Kepler orbit in a repulsive Coulomb field.
breaks: Gravity has only one sign of charge, so it has no screening, no dipole radiation and no gravitational conductor. Gravitational charge also equals inertial mass, which has no electric counterpart.

name: Larmor radiation and the collapse of classical atoms
summary: An electron on a classical Kepler orbit around a nucleus radiates at the Larmor rate and spirals inward within about 10⁻¹¹ s. This failure of Rutherford's planetary atom motivated Bohr's stationary orbits. The same radiative decay of orbits shapes cyclotron and synchrotron motion.
breaks: In quantum mechanics there is no continuous inspiral. Stationary states replace it, and radiation occurs only in transitions at discrete frequencies.

name: Field momentum restores momentum conservation
summary: Magnetic forces between moving charges violate Newton's third law, so mechanical momentum alone is not conserved. Maxwell's theory restores conservation of linear and angular momentum by giving the field a momentum density ε0E×B and a stress tensor. Feynman's disk paradox and hidden momentum are standard examples.
breaks: Inside matter, how momentum splits between the field and the medium is ambiguous; this is the Abraham–Minkowski controversy.

name: Galilean kinematics vs Lorentz-covariant electrodynamics
summary: Maxwell's equations are not invariant under Galilean boosts, as the magnet-and-conductor asymmetry and the fixed speed of light show. Resolving this clash with Newtonian kinematics produced the Lorentz transformations and Einstein's 1905 relativity. Under relativity, Newton's second law becomes the covariant Lorentz-force equation.

name: Foucault pendulum and Rytov rotation: one holonomy
summary: Each day, the Foucault pendulum's swing plane turns by the solid angle 2π(1−cosϑ) enclosed by the local vertical, where ϑ is the colatitude; this is parallel transport on a sphere. The polarization of light in a helically coiled fibre rotates by the solid angle swept by its propagation direction (the Rytov–Vladimirskii rotation, observed by Tomita and Chiao). Both are the same geometric phase.
breaks: The pendulum carries a classical vector across Earth's surface. For photons the rotation is a helicity-dependent Berry phase ±σΩ, with opposite signs for the two circular polarizations.

name: Larmor's theorem: Coriolis force mimics a magnetic field
summary: In a frame rotating at Ω, the Coriolis force 2m v×Ω has the same form as the magnetic force q v×B. Rotating at Ω=−qB/2m therefore removes a weak uniform field to first order, which explains the Larmor precession of orbits and atomic diamagnetism. Conversely, rotating neutral systems can simulate magnetic fields.
breaks: The equivalence holds only to first order. The rotating frame adds a centrifugal force of order Ω² with no magnetic counterpart, which must be small or cancelled by a trap.

name: Optical bistability and the Ikeda route to chaos
summary: A cavity filled with a Kerr medium has an S-shaped transmission curve bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations, which gives hysteresis and optical switching. Ikeda showed that the delayed ring-cavity map period-doubles into chaos as the input power rises, a Feigenbaum cascade realized in optics.
sources: Feigenbaum (1978). "Quantitative universality for a class of nonlinear transformations". *J. Stat. Phys.* 19, 25. [doi:10.1007/BF01020332](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01020332)

name: Lorenz–Haken: single-mode laser equals Lorenz system
summary: Haken (1975) showed that the Maxwell–Bloch equations of a homogeneously broadened single-mode laser (field, polarization, inversion) are isomorphic to Lorenz's convection model. A bad-cavity laser pumped far above threshold therefore shows Lorenz chaos, which has been observed in far-infrared NH3 lasers. Class-B lasers reach chaos when modulation or delayed feedback is added.
breaks: Lorenz chaos needs the bad-cavity condition σ>b+1 and pumping many times above threshold, which ordinary lasers never reach. For convection the three-mode equations are a severe truncation, while for the laser they are close to exact.

name: Ray chaos in deformed optical microcavities
summary: Rays in a dielectric microdisk follow billiard orbits. Deforming the circle breaks the KAM tori, and whispering-gallery rays then diffuse chaotically in the Poincaré surface of section until they drop below the critical angle and refract out. This explains the directional emission and spoiled Q of asymmetric-resonant-cavity lasers.
breaks: When kR is not large, wave effects such as dynamical tunnelling and scarred modes modify the ray picture.

name: Optical fibres as a testbed for NLS rogue waves
summary: Deep-water wave groups and fibre pulses both obey the focusing NLS. Benjamin–Feir modulational instability, Akhmediev breathers and the Peregrine soliton, all proposed prototypes of rogue waves, have therefore been generated in optical fibres and water tanks with the same normalized solutions. Optical rogue waves also appear in supercontinuum generation.
breaks: Ocean waves add higher-order (Dysthe) corrections, directional spreading and breaking, so it is contested whether real rogue waves are NLS breathers rather than linear focusing. Fibres add Raman effects and higher-order dispersion.

name: Optical solitons from the integrable NLS equation
summary: A pulse envelope in a Kerr fibre with anomalous dispersion obeys the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which inverse scattering solves exactly. Self-phase modulation balances group-velocity dispersion, and the fundamental sech soliton (N=1) and the higher-order breathers are the same objects found in deep-water wave groups.
breaks: Real fibres add loss, the Raman self-frequency shift and higher-order dispersion, all of which break integrability. Solitons then shed dispersive waves and undergo fission, which is what drives supercontinuum generation.
sources: Zabusky & Kruskal (1965). "Interaction of 'Solitons' in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 15, 240. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.240)

Gardner, Greene, Kruskal & Miura (1967). "Method for Solving the Korteweg-deVries Equation". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 19, 1095. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.19.1095)

name: Lugiato–Lefever patterns and Kerr microcombs
summary: A continuously driven Kerr microresonator obeys the Lugiato–Lefever equation, a damped and driven NLS first derived for transverse optical patterns. Its Turing instability creates the primary comb (Turing rolls). Coexistence of homogeneous and localized states yields dissipative Kerr solitons, which are the mode-locked microcombs.
sources: Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

name: Injection locking of lasers follows the Adler equation
summary: A slave laser injected with weak light from a master laser phase-locks when the detuning lies inside the locking range. It follows the Adler equation of phase synchronization, the same one that describes Huygens clocks and Kuramoto oscillators. Coupled laser arrays show Kuramoto-type synchronization transitions, and mode-locking is the phase locking of many cavity modes.
breaks: In semiconductor lasers, the linewidth-enhancement factor couples amplitude to phase. This skews the locking range and can cause instabilities that the pure phase model does not capture.
sources: Strogatz (2000). "From Kuramoto to Crawford: exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators". *Physica D* 143, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4)

name: Cavity modes and LC lines as mechanical oscillators
summary: Each normal mode of a resonant cavity obeys a damped driven oscillator equation, with the quality factor Q=ω0/Δω defined exactly as for a mechanical resonator. A lumped LC transmission line is a mass–spring chain (L↔m, 1/C↔k): it has the same discrete-lattice dispersion and cutoff, and its continuum limit is the same wave equation.
map: \ddot a+\frac{\omega_0}{Q}\dot a+\omega_0^2a=f(t);\ L\leftrightarrow m,\ C^{-1}\leftrightarrow k,\ R\leftrightarrow b;\ \omega(k)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{LC}}\left|\sin\frac{ka}{2}\right|
breaks: The analogy holds mode by mode, but not for the field's spatial structure. Cavity modes carry polarization and vector boundary conditions, and their density grows as ω², which a scalar chain does not reproduce.

name: Coupled-mode theory: directional couplers as coupled pendula
summary: Two evanescently coupled waveguides exchange power along z exactly as two weakly coupled identical pendula exchange energy in time (beats). Detuning gives incomplete transfer and an avoided crossing of the supermodes. Arrays of waveguides or ring resonators are oscillator chains, with tight-binding dispersion and discrete diffraction.
map: i\frac{da_{1,2}}{dz}=\beta a_{1,2}+\kappa a_{2,1}\ \Rightarrow\ P_2(z)=\sin^2\kappa z;\qquad \beta(k)=\beta_0+2\kappa\cos kd
breaks: Propagation distance plays the role of time. The coupled-mode equations are first order and Schrödinger-like, the rotating-wave limit of the second-order pendulum equations.

name: Fano lines and plasmon hybridization from coupled oscillators
summary: Two coupled damped oscillators, a broad bright mode driven by light and a narrow dark mode, produce an asymmetric Fano line with a transparency window. This is the standard classical model of plasmon-induced transparency in metamaterials. Coupled nanoparticle plasmons split into bonding and antibonding hybrid modes just as coupled pendula do.
map: \ddot x_1+\gamma_1\dot x_1+\omega_1^2x_1-\kappa x_2=\frac{F}{m}e^{-i\omega t},\quad \ddot x_2+\gamma_2\dot x_2+\omega_2^2x_2-\kappa x_1=0,\ \gamma_2\ll\gamma_1
breaks: In atomic EIT, the dark mode is a quantum superposition of ground states prepared by a control laser. The classical model reproduces the lineshape and dispersion, but not storage of a quantum state.

name: Topological bands of coupled resonators and spring lattices
summary: Topological photonics treats lattices of coupled resonators and waveguides as normal-mode problems whose bands carry winding or Chern numbers. Applying the same band topology to coupled pendula, gyroscope lattices and spring networks gives mechanical topological insulators and edge modes in isostatic lattices. SSH-chain edge states appear in both.
breaks: Mechanical lattices are second order in time (an ω² eigenproblem) and have no Fermi level, and modes protected by time reversal need engineered pseudospins. Robust one-way edge modes require broken time reversal, for example spinning gyroscopes or magneto-optic media.

name: Lorentz–Drude oscillator model of dielectric response
summary: Treating bound electrons as driven damped oscillators gives the Lorentz permittivity: normal dispersion below resonance, and absorption with anomalous dispersion at resonance. Setting the spring constant to zero gives the Drude metal with plasma frequency ωp. Causality of the oscillator's response yields the Kramers–Kronig relations.
breaks: The resonance frequencies and oscillator strengths f_j come from quantum transitions. The classical model gets the functional form right but cannot supply these parameters.

name: Split-ring and plasmon resonators as damped oscillators
summary: A split-ring resonator is an LC circuit. Its Lorentzian response gives an effective permeability that turns negative just above resonance, which is the route to negative-index media. A localized surface plasmon is a nanoparticle's conduction-electron cloud oscillating against the restoring field of its own surface charge; it resonates at the Fröhlich condition, at ωp/√3 for a Drude sphere in vacuum.
breaks: Plasmon damping includes Landau damping and surface scattering, and very small particles show quantum size effects. A single classical oscillator misses all of these.

name: Radiation reaction as oscillator damping
summary: A charged oscillator loses energy at the Larmor rate. For near-harmonic motion the Abraham–Lorentz force mτ0 d³x/dt³ reduces to a damping rate γ=ω0²τ0. This gives the classical natural linewidth Δλ=(4π/3)re≈1.2×10⁻¹⁴ m, independent of frequency.
breaks: Taken exactly, the third-order Abraham–Lorentz equation has runaway solutions and preacceleration, so it is used only perturbatively (the Landau–Lifshitz form). For atoms, quantum linewidths replace the classical value.
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)

name: Rayleigh and Thomson scattering from a driven electron
summary: When light drives a bound electron, the scattering cross-section is the square of the oscillator's response. Far below resonance it rises as ω⁴ (Rayleigh scattering, the blue sky); far above, it tends to the frequency-independent Thomson value; near ω0 it shows a Lorentzian resonance peak.
breaks: At photon energies comparable to mc², Thomson scattering gives way to Compton scattering, with recoil and the Klein–Nishina cross-section, which the classical oscillator cannot produce.

name: Impedance, reflection and waveguide cutoff for sound and light
summary: For both sound and light, normal-incidence reflection follows from impedance mismatch: r=(Z2−Z1)/(Z2+Z1), with Z=ρc for sound and Z=√(μ/ε) for light. Quarter-wave matching layers on ultrasound transducers work like anti-reflection coatings. Acoustic ducts carry higher modes with cutoff frequencies and evanescent tails, as metal waveguides do.
breaks: Sound in a fluid is a scalar longitudinal wave. A rigid duct therefore carries a plane mode with no cutoff, which a hollow metal guide lacks because it has no TEM mode, and sound has no polarization or TE/TM split. Elastic solids add shear waves, and P–S mode conversion at interfaces.

name: Acoustic metamaterials and transformation acoustics
summary: Ideas from electromagnetic metamaterials carried over to sound. Locally resonant inclusions give negative effective mass density or bulk modulus, producing double-negative acoustic media, and phononic crystals mirror photonic band gaps. Because the 2D acoustic equations are form-invariant, Pendry-style transformation cloaks can be built for sound, with density playing the role of permeability and compressibility that of permittivity.
map: \rho\leftrightarrow\mu,\ \ K^{-1}\leftrightarrow\varepsilon\ \ (\text{2D, one polarization});\quad \rho_{eff}(\omega)<0\ \text{just above a local resonance}
breaks: Full elastodynamics, which includes shear waves, is not form-invariant under coordinate transformations, so elastic cloaks need exotic Willis-type media. Sound has no polarization, and acoustic metamaterials are often lossy and narrowband.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)

name: Brillouin scattering couples light to sound
summary: Light Bragg-reflects off an acoustic wave and is Doppler-shifted by the sound frequency. At high intensity, electrostriction drives the acoustic wave itself, giving stimulated Brillouin scattering. For narrow-linewidth light this is the lowest-threshold fibre nonlinearity, with a shift of about 11 GHz in silica at 1550 nm, and it is used in Brillouin lasers, slow light and distributed strain sensing.

name: Mach cone and Cherenkov cone
summary: A source that outruns the waves it emits builds a conical wavefront from the Huygens envelope. A supersonic body gives the Mach cone, and a charge moving faster than c/n gives the Cherenkov cone. The geometry is the same once c_s is replaced by c/n.
breaks: Cherenkov light is linear radiation from a charge in a dispersive dielectric. It is emitted only at frequencies where n(ω)>1/β, with a Frank–Tamm spectrum proportional to ω. A sonic boom is instead a nonlinear shock (an N-wave) from a body displacing fluid.

name: Paul traps evade Earnshaw by Mathieu stabilization
summary: Earnshaw's theorem, which says Laplace's equation allows no potential minimum, forbids trapping charges with static electric fields. An rf quadrupole makes each coordinate obey a Mathieu equation whose stability region gives dynamic confinement. This Kapitza-pendulum mechanism is behind ion traps and quadrupole mass filters.

name: Laser as a Van der Pol self-sustained oscillator
summary: Semiclassically, the single-mode laser field is a Van der Pol oscillator. Gain acts as negative damping, threshold is a Hopf bifurcation, and gain saturation fixes a limit-cycle amplitude while leaving the phase free. The output is a self-sustained oscillator whose phase diffusion sets the Schawlow–Townes linewidth.
map: \ddot x-\mu(1-x^2)\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0\ \leftrightarrow\ \dot{\mathcal E}=\tfrac12(G-\kappa)\mathcal E-\beta|\mathcal E|^2\mathcal E
breaks: The phase diffusion that sets the linewidth is driven by spontaneous emission, a quantum noise source that the deterministic Van der Pol equation does not contain. Multimode and class-B lasers add relaxation oscillations and mode competition.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Anharmonic electron oscillator model of χ(2) and χ(3)
summary: Adding quadratic and cubic terms to the Lorentz oscillator produces harmonics and an intensity-dependent response. An asymmetric x² restoring force gives χ(2), which vanishes for centrosymmetric potentials. A Duffing x³ term gives χ(3): the Kerr index n2 (an amplitude-dependent frequency) and third-harmonic generation. The model also yields Miller's rule.
breaks: Real nonlinear susceptibilities come from quantum transition matrix elements. They also have non-electronic sources (Raman, orientational, thermal) that a single oscillator leaves out.
sources: Franken et al. (1961). "Generation of Optical Harmonics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 7, 118. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118)

name: Optical parametric amplification as parametric resonance
summary: A pump wave modulating a χ(2) medium amplifies a signal and an idler with ωs+ωi=ωp. The degenerate case ωs=ωp/2 is the parametric resonance of a swing pumped at twice its natural frequency. It shares the phase-sensitive gain (one quadrature amplified, the other deamplified) and exponential growth above threshold, and the OPO is its self-oscillating form.
breaks: Optical parametric gain needs phase matching across a propagating medium, a spatial condition that a single swing has no counterpart for. The non-degenerate case couples two distinct modes.

name: Kapitza effective potential is the ponderomotive energy
summary: Averaging motion in a rapidly oscillating force F0 cos ωt gives Kapitza's effective potential F0²/4mω². For an electron in a laser field this is the ponderomotive energy Up. It sets the strong-field scales of attosecond physics, including the high-harmonic cutoff Ip+3.17Up, and it pushes electrons out of intense foci.
breaks: The averaging requires the field to vary slowly in space over one quiver excursion. At relativistic intensities (a0≳1), magnetic forces and the relativistic mass increase modify Up.
sources: Krausz & Ivanov (2009). "Attosecond physics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 163. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.163)

name: Sagnac interferometers as optical gyroscopes
summary: Beams sent both ways around a loop rotating at Ω pick up a phase difference proportional to the enclosed area, which gives an absolute measurement of rotation. Ring-laser and fibre-optic gyroscopes built on this effect have largely replaced spinning-rotor gyroscopes in inertial navigation. Large ring lasers resolve Earth's rotation.
breaks: The optical device has no angular momentum. It senses rotation through the light travel time in the rotating frame, not through gyroscopic rigidity, so it shows no precession or nutation and needs no spin-up.

name: Larmor precession of magnetic moments as a gyroscope
summary: A magnetic dipole tied to angular momentum, μ=γL, feels the torque μ×B and precesses about B at ωL=γB. This is the same equation that makes a heavy top precess under the torque of gravity. The gyroscopic picture underlies NMR, ESR and MRI.
map: \frac{d\mathbf L}{dt}=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B=-\gamma\mathbf B\times\mathbf L\ \leftrightarrow\ \frac{d\mathbf L}{dt}=\mathbf r\times m\mathbf g;\quad \omega_L=\gamma B,\ \Omega_{top}=\frac{mgr}{L}
breaks: The magnetic torque scales with L, so the Larmor frequency does not depend on the size of the spin; a top, by contrast, precesses more slowly the faster it spins. The top's steady precession is also only the fast-spin approximation, with nutation added on top.

name: Quadrupole moment is the traceless inertia tensor
summary: For a mass distribution the quadrupole tensor equals tr(I)δij−3Iij, so a body's principal moments fix its far gravitational field (MacCullagh's formula). Torques from the Sun and Moon on Earth's quadrupole cause the precession of the equinoxes, and the same J2 term makes satellite orbits precess.
breaks: Mass is never negative and the mass dipole vanishes about the centre of mass, so the gravitational expansion has no dipole term, unlike the electric case.

name: Laser linewidth sets temporal coherence
summary: By the Wiener–Khinchin theorem the coherence time is the inverse spectral width, so the Schawlow–Townes linewidth fixes a laser's coherence length. Above threshold the intensity statistics change from thermal (g2(0)=2) to Poissonian (g2(0)=1), which separates a laser from a filtered thermal source of the same bandwidth.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Dynamic light scattering via intensity correlations
summary: Light scattered by many diffusing particles forms a fluctuating Gaussian speckle field. The Siegert relation then gives the field correlation from the measured intensity correlation, and its decay rate Dq² yields particle size via Stokes–Einstein. This is the Hanbury Brown–Twiss intensity-correlation method of statistical optics applied to scattering.
breaks: The Siegert relation holds only for Gaussian (many-scatterer) fields. Few scatterers, non-ergodic samples or multiple scattering (which needs diffusing-wave spectroscopy) break it.

name: Superlenses beat the diffraction limit via evanescent waves
summary: Fourier optics locates the diffraction limit: spatial frequencies above nk0 are evanescent and never reach the far field. Pendry's n=−1 slab amplifies these components and restores them in the image. Silver superlenses and hyperbolic hyperlenses achieve partial versions.
breaks: Absorption and any deviation from ε=−1 limit the amplification, so resolution degrades with loss. The effect works only in the near field, within a fraction of a wavelength.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)

name: Space–time duality: diffraction ↔ dispersion
summary: The paraxial diffraction equation for a beam and the pulse equation with group-velocity dispersion are the same Schrödinger-type equation, with transverse position swapped for retarded time. A quadratic temporal phase therefore acts as a 'time lens'. Stretchers, compressors (as used in chirped-pulse amplification), temporal imaging and the time–bandwidth product are the temporal counterparts of Fresnel propagation, lenses and the space–bandwidth limit.
breaks: Time is one-dimensional and causal. Diffraction matches only anomalous dispersion, while dispersion can take either sign and has higher orders (β3) with no diffraction counterpart. Time lenses need electro-optic or nonlinear phase modulation, not glass.
sources: Strickland & Mourou (1985). "Compression of amplified chirped optical pulses". *Opt. Commun.* 56, 219. [doi:10.1016/0030-4018(85)90120-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/0030-4018(85)90120-8)

name: Diffraction imaging: scattering amplitude as Fourier transform
summary: In the first Born approximation the far-field scattering amplitude is the Fourier transform of the scatterer's density at q=k_out−k_in. X-ray and coherent diffraction imaging are thus Fourier optics with the phase lost, recovered by oversampled phase retrieval or by a holographic reference wave (Gabor).
map: f(\mathbf q)\propto\int\rho(\mathbf r)e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}d^3r,\qquad |\mathbf q|=2k\sin(\theta/2)
breaks: Valid only for weak single scattering. Multiple scattering and absorption (dynamical diffraction) break the plain Fourier relation, and detectors record only |f|².
sources: Gabor (1948). "A New Microscopic Principle". *Nature* 161, 777. [doi:10.1038/161777a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/161777a0)

name: Ray optics as the eikonal limit of Maxwell waves
summary: Writing the field as a slowly varying amplitude times e^{ik_0S} and keeping leading order in λ/L reduces the wave equation to the eikonal equation. Its characteristics are rays obeying Fermat's principle, the next order gives intensity transport along ray tubes, and Snell's law is the interface limit of the plane-wave boundary conditions.
breaks: Fails near caustics, foci, shadow edges and features ≲λ, where diffraction (Kirchhoff, Keller's GTD) is needed. Polarization appears only at the next order (Rytov rotation).

name: Resonator stability and Gaussian beams via ABCD matrices
summary: Paraxial ray-transfer matrices decide whether a laser cavity is stable: rays stay bounded over many round trips if and only if |A+D|/2≤1, i.e. 0≤g1g2≤1. Kogelnik's ABCD law propagates the Gaussian beam's complex q parameter with the same matrices, which gives the cavity's mode size and waist.

name: Generalized Snell's law and negative refraction
summary: Snell's law follows from continuity of the tangential phase. With n<0 the refracted ray bends to the same side of the normal (Veselago). A metasurface's abrupt phase gradient dΦ/dx adds tangential momentum, giving the generalized laws of reflection and refraction behind flat lenses. Graded-index designs (Luneburg lens, Maxwell fish-eye) are the ray limit of transformation optics.

name: Thin films are transmission-line impedance transformers
summary: At normal incidence, waves in layered dielectrics obey the same transfer-matrix (telegrapher) equations as a transmission line with impedance Z0/n. A quarter-wave antireflection coating is therefore a quarter-wave matching transformer, and a Bragg mirror is a periodic line with a stop band.
breaks: At oblique incidence the effective impedance depends on polarization (s: Z∝1/(n cosθ), p: Z∝cosθ/n), so a coating designed for one angle and polarization is mismatched for others.

name: Laser cavity as Fabry–Pérot; Fox–Li diffraction modes
summary: A laser resonator is a Fabry–Pérot interferometer with gain: its longitudinal modes are the transmission peaks spaced by the free spectral range, and its passive linewidth is FSR divided by finesse. Fox and Li obtained the transverse modes as self-reproducing patterns of repeated Fresnel diffraction between the mirrors, with diffraction loss set by the Fresnel number.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Smith–Purcell radiation: a grating equation for moving charges
summary: A charge skimming a periodic grating radiates because the grating's reciprocal vectors couple its evanescent, slower-than-light field to free-space waves. The emitted wavelength obeys the grating equation with the source's phase velocity set by the electron speed. This is Cherenkov phase matching with grating momentum in place of the medium's index.

name: Antenna arrays and apertures are Fraunhofer diffraction
summary: A phased array's far field is the element pattern times an array factor that is the N-slit grating function. A progressive phase steers the main lobe, just as oblique incidence shifts a grating's orders. An aperture antenna's pattern is the Fraunhofer transform of its aperture field, so its beamwidth is the same λ/D as a diffraction-limited lens.

name: Faraday rotation and c=1/√(ε0μ0): light joins EM
summary: Faraday's 1845 discovery that a magnetic field rotates the plane of polarization was the first evidence that light is electromagnetic. Maxwell's displacement current then predicted transverse waves at 1/√(ε0μ0), matching the measured speed of light, so polarization became the direction of the transverse E field.
sources: Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)

name: Crystal optics from the dielectric tensor
summary: Birefringence is the anisotropic linear response of fields in matter. A symmetric tensor ε_ij makes D non-parallel to E, so the Poynting vector walks off from k, and each propagation direction has two orthogonally polarized eigenmodes, organized by the index ellipsoid. Crystal symmetry fixes whether the medium is isotropic, uniaxial or biaxial.
